title: Ar-Ra'uf, the Most Kind
hookLine: the Most Kind, tender in compassion
tomorrow: Eli says a wall belongs to whoever paints it. whose wall is it?

lines: CUT THEM OFF, OR BE KIND?
cards: Two lines go around online. One says: protect your peace, cut them off. The other says: be kind, everyone's carrying something.
Yesterday's question lives right between them. Is tenderness toward someone who wronged you a strength, or a leak? Today's Name is Ar-Ra'uf, the Most Kind, tender in compassion.
And scholars of the Names read this word in two different ways. Both deserve a hearing.

teach.b: Start with the verse. In Pickthall's words: "Lo! Allah is full of pity, Merciful toward mankind." Ra'uf and Rahim, side by side.
So if Allah is already the Merciful, what does Ra'uf add? The first reading says: degree.

teach.h: ONE READING: MERCY TURNED ALL THE WAY UP.
teach.b: Ra'fa is rahma turned all the way up, mercy at its most intense and most tender. Al-Ghazali, in his book on the Names, describes it this way. On this view, tenderness isn't a weak form of mercy.
It's the strongest. The second reading says: direction.

teach.h: THE OTHER: MERCY THAT LIFTS A BURDEN.
teach.b: Other commentators hear ra'fa as the mercy that lifts a burden and keeps hardship away, while rahma can include a good that stings, like medicine.

They point to a verse about the Prophet, peace be upon him: "unto whom aught that ye are overburdened is grievous, full of concern for you, for the believers full of pity, merciful." Your weight is heavy on him.
On this view, tenderness is precise: it notices exactly what someone is carrying. And here's the detail to tell a friend tonight.

teach.h: THE SAME TWO WORDS, FOR THE PROPHET.
teach.b: In that verse, the Qur'an describes the Prophet with the same two words it uses for God, ra'uf and rahim.
Neither reading makes tender mean silent. The one described as full of pity is the same one who delivered the hardest messages.

how: Some Muslims call on Allah with paired Names, as the Qur'an pairs them: ya Ra'uf, ya Rahim, O Most Kind, O Most Merciful.

o: the Most Patient, slow to anger
the Most Kind, tender in compassion
the Most Gentle, never stern at all

games.q: two readings of one Name — tap the pairs.
p: the Most Kind, tender in compassion
your weight is heavy on him

s: Ra'uf is simply another word for Rahim, adding nothing
scholars read something extra in it: mercy at full strength, or mercy that lifts a burden.
the Qur'an describes the Prophet with ra'uf and rahim, words it also uses for God
"for the believers full of pity, merciful."
being tender with someone means never telling them a hard truth
the one described as full of pity also delivered the hardest messages.

games.q: you read ra'fa as mercy that lifts a burden. your friend reads it as mercy turned all the way up. what's the best case for your friend's side?
o: if mercy has degrees, tender is its strongest setting, so it can't be weak.
tender means you never say anything hard to anyone at all.
both readings say the same thing, so there's really nothing to argue.
games.why: the first reading, given by al-Ghazali, makes tenderness the peak of mercy. the second sees mercy aimed at someone's weight. both are real readings; neither makes tender mean silent.

practice: Bring to mind one person carrying something heavy right now: a friend mid-exams, a parent who's tired, a neighbor who's alone. Write them a short, tender text, with no advice and no fixing, only that you noticed.
Send it, or keep it ready, and let them stay in mind for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Ar-Ra'uf. The Most Kind: mercy at its most tender, the kind that feels the weight someone is carrying.

orig.note: Arabic: the Most Kind, a Name of Allah; the Qur'an pairs it with Rahim, Merciful.

carryVoice: Your line: tender, which isn't the same thing as silent, and is never the same as weak. See you tomorrow.
